why_how.text: Road rage happening right now is reported by calling nine one one at once.
A useful report gives where the vehicles were last seen, the plate, the direction, the road, colors, weapons and what happened.

scenario.text: Raj sees a driver ram another car in anger on the highway right in front of him.

reasoning.text: Road rage that is happening right now is reported by calling nine one one at once.

result.text: Raj, once safely able, calls nine one one immediately.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a witnessed aggressive driving act needs a different number from road rage in progress.

correction.text: The same emergency number, nine one one, is used for road rage in progress and for a witnessed aggressive driving act.

memory_support.text: Rage on the road: call nine one one.

prompt.text: You witnessed an aggressive driving act. Which details does the dispatcher need?

answer.text: Where the vehicles were last seen, the plate if known, the direction and road, colors, weapons, what happened and your role.

rationale.text: A report of an aggressive driving act gives location, plate, direction, road, colors, weapons, what happened and whether you were a victim or witness.

narration.text: Welcome to the section on decisions, distraction and respectful driving. We begin with something you hope never to need: reporting road rage and aggressive driving. The guide explains when to call, what details to give, and why reports from residents matter. It is short, but the details matter, because a clear report helps officers respond. After this lesson, the section moves on to how you make decisions, how distraction works, and how to share the road responsibly. To remember: road rage in progress; what to tell dispatchers; why your report matters.

lines.text: Call nine one one at once.

narration.text: Report road rage that is happening right now by calling nine one one at once. The same number is used to report an aggressive driving act that you witness. So there is no separate line to remember for these situations; both go to the emergency number. Make the call when it is safe to do so, without taking your attention from your own driving. A quick, clear call is the most useful thing a witness can do for everyone else on the road. To remember: road rage happening now; call nine one one at once; same number for aggressive acts.

lines.text: Where the vehicles were last seen.

narration.text: When you call about an aggressive driving act, give the details the guide lists. Say where the vehicles were last seen, the license plate if you know it, the direction of travel and the road. Describe the vehicle colors and any weapons. Explain what happened and whether you were a victim or a witness. Those details let officers find the right vehicle and understand the situation quickly, so think through them in order as you speak. To remember: where the vehicles were last seen; plate, direction, road, colors; weapons, what happened, your role.

lines.text: Trap: aggressive acts need another number.
Road rage in progress: nine one one.
Witnessed aggressive act: also nine one one.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because road rage in progress feels like an emergency and a witnessed aggressive act may not, some people assume the two need different numbers. The guide uses one. Road rage in progress goes straight to nine one one, and the same number is used to report a witnessed aggressive driving act. So whichever situation a question describes, the reporting number is the same. Only the details you give change with what you saw. To remember: road rage in progress: nine one one; witnessed aggressive act: also nine one one.

Here is a quick check: you witnessed an aggressive driving act and you have called nine one one. What details does the dispatcher need from you? Think it through before the answer. The guide lists them. Give where the vehicles were last seen, the plate if you know it, the direction of travel and the road, the vehicle colors, any weapons, what happened, and whether you were a victim or a witness. Clear facts in that order make the report useful. A helpful hook for this lesson: rage on the road: call nine one one. In short: a report of an aggressive driving act gives location, plate, direction, road, colors, weapons, what happened and whether you were a victim or witness.

lines.text: Road rage now: nine one one.

narration.text: To wrap up, report road rage that is happening right now by calling nine one one at once, and use the same number to report a witnessed aggressive driving act. Give where the vehicles were last seen, the plate if known, the direction, the road, the colors, any weapons, what happened and whether you were a victim or witness. Cutting road rage and aggressive driving is central to the Washington State Patrol's mission, and reports from residents help improve safety. To remember: road rage now: nine one one; give location, plate, direction, details; reports help the State Patrol.

why_how.text: Informed decisions weigh every factor before you act and lower the risk of crashes.
The guide's approach is to inform yourself and others, prepare your position and speed, and then make a final check.

scenario.text: Tom wants to change lanes to pass a slow truck.

reasoning.text: Inform yourself with mirror checks and signal, prepare the vehicle's position and speed, then make a final check before the maneuver.

result.text: Tom checks mirrors and signals, sets his speed and position, makes a final check, then changes lanes.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the final check comes first in the decision approach.

correction.text: The final check comes last, after informing yourself and others and preparing position and speed, right before the maneuver.

memory_support.text: Inform, prepare, then a final check.

prompt.text: In the guide's decision approach, which step comes right before the maneuver?

rationale.text: The final check comes last, after informing yourself and others and preparing your position and speed.

narration.text: This lesson covers how drivers make decisions. The guide starts with the idea of an informed decision, then looks at what shapes your decisions, including age and experience. It then gives a three-step approach for any maneuver, a set of qualities every change should have, and the basic ways to solve a problem on the road. Decision-making can sound abstract, but the guide turns it into steps you can practice on every drive. To remember: informed decisions; what shapes them; a three-step approach. A helpful hook for this lesson: inform, prepare, then a final check.

An informed decision weighs every factor before you act. The guide says such decisions raise your awareness, encourage responsible driving and lower the risk of crashes. Your decisions are shaped by three things: your knowledge of traffic laws, your experience with safe practices, and the capabilities that come with your age and brain development. So learning the rules, practicing safe habits and understanding your own stage of development all feed into better decisions. To remember: weigh every factor before acting; raises awareness; lowers crash risk.

lines.text: Safety ahead of speed and peers.

narration.text: Age affects decisions in different ways. In teen drivers, the brain area that handles judgment and decisions is still maturing, so teens may take more risks or misjudge situations, and they must put safety ahead of speed and peer pressure. For older drivers, physical and mental abilities shift with age, and older drivers can be hurt more seriously in crashes. Yet many stay safe and capable drivers late in life. The reasons for extra care differ by age. To remember: teen judgment area still maturing; safety ahead of speed and peers; older drivers: abilities shift.

The guide's decision approach has three steps. First, inform yourself with mirror checks and signal your plan to others. Second, prepare the vehicle so you reach the hazard at the right position and speed. Third, make a final check before the maneuver. Throughout, aim to be aware, predictable and smooth in every change you make on the road. These steps work for lane changes, turns and any other maneuver where others need to know what you are doing. To remember: inform yourself; signal your plan; prepare position and speed; final check before the maneuver.

lines.text: Trap: the final check comes first.
Final check last, before the move.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The word check makes some learners place the final check at the start. In the guide's decision approach, the final check comes last, after informing yourself and others and after preparing your position and speed, right before the maneuver. So the order is inform, prepare, then check. The first step also involves checks, your mirrors, but the final check is a separate last look just before you commit to the move. To remember: inform, then prepare; final check last, before the move. A helpful hook for this lesson: inform, prepare, then a final check.

When something on the road needs a response, the guide says solving the problem usually means changing your speed, shifting your lane position, or changing your path to reach a safe place to reassess. Whatever you choose, tell others your plan so you do not surprise them. That links back to the three-step approach: signaling and moving predictably let other drivers react to you smoothly instead of being caught off guard by a sudden move. To remember: change your speed; shift your lane position; change path; tell others.

lines.text: Which step comes right before the move?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: in the guide's three-step decision approach, which step comes right before the maneuver itself? Decide before the answer, and remember the trap about the word check. The first step is informing yourself and signaling, and the second is preparing position and speed. The answer is the final check. It comes last, after informing and preparing, as a final look just before you change lanes or turn. A helpful hook for this lesson: inform, prepare, then a final check. In short: the final check comes last, after informing yourself and others and preparing your position and speed.

lines.text: Teens and older drivers: different reasons.

narration.text: To sum up, informed decisions weigh every factor and lower crash risk, and they are shaped by your knowledge, experience and development. Teens must put safety ahead of speed and peer pressure because their judgment center is still maturing, while older drivers face changing abilities yet often stay capable. Use the three steps, inform, prepare, final check, aim to be aware, predictable and smooth, and solve problems by changing speed, position or path while telling others your plan. To remember: weigh every factor; teens and older drivers: different reasons; inform, prepare, final check.

why_how.text: The OODA loop is Observe, Orient, Decide, Act, and each situation leads straight into the next.
Orient is the understanding step, where you judge what a change means for safety.

scenario.text: Ella sees brake lights flash several cars ahead of her on the freeway.

reasoning.text: Observe spots what changed, Orient judges what it means for safety, Decide picks the safest action, and Act carries it out smoothly.

result.text: Ella notices the lights, understands traffic is slowing, chooses to ease off, and slows smoothly with her brake lights warning others.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking Observe and Orient are the same step.

correction.text: Observe is noticing that something changed, whereas Orient is working out what that change means before you Decide.

prompt.text: Which OODA step is working out what a change means for your safety?

rationale.text: Orient uses your knowledge to judge what a change means for safety, after Observe has noticed it.

narration.text: This lesson introduces the OODA loop, a way of thinking through situations as they unfold. OODA stands for Observe, Orient, Decide, Act. The guide calls it a loop because each situation leads straight into the next one, so you are always cycling through it as you drive. We will look at what happens in each of the four steps and spend extra time on the difference between the first two, which learners often blur together. To remember: observe, Orient, Decide, Act; why it is a loop; observe versus Orient. A helpful hook for this lesson: notice, understand, choose, do.

lines.text: Decide and Act: choose, then do.

narration.text: In the OODA loop, Observe spots what changed. Orient uses your knowledge to judge what the change means for safety. Decide picks the safest action. Act carries it out smoothly with clear signals. Then the loop begins again, because the situation has changed once more. So driving becomes a steady cycle: notice, understand, choose and do, over and over, each pass shaped by what happened in the one before. To remember: observe: spot what changed; orient: judge what it means; decide and Act: choose, then do. A helpful hook for this lesson: notice, understand, choose, do.

lines.text: Trap: Observe and Orient are one step.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Observe and Orient both happen in your head, quickly, so learners often merge them. The guide keeps them apart. Observe is noticing that something changed, whereas Orient is working out what that change means for your safety and others before you Decide. Seeing brake lights ahead is Observe. Realizing that traffic is slowing and you may need to slow too is Orient. Only after Orient can you Decide well. To remember: observe: notice the change; orient: understand what it means. A helpful hook for this lesson: notice, understand, choose, do.

Here is a quick check: which step of the OODA loop is the one where you work out what a change means for your safety? Decide before the answer, and remember the trap. The first step only notices that something changed. The answer is Orient. Orient uses your knowledge to judge what the change means, after Observe has spotted it and before Decide picks the safest action. Act then carries the choice out smoothly with clear signals. A helpful hook for this lesson: notice, understand, choose, do. In short: orient uses your knowledge to judge what a change means for safety, after Observe has noticed it.

lines.text: Each situation leads to the next.

narration.text: The OODA loop is called a loop because each situation leads straight into the next one. After you Act, something new has changed, so you Observe again, Orient again, and so on. That is why the Act step stresses carrying out your choice smoothly with clear signals. A smooth, signaled action gives other drivers a clear picture, which makes the next turn of the loop easier for everyone, including you. To remember: each situation leads to the next; you cycle through it constantly; act smoothly, with clear signals. A helpful hook for this lesson: notice, understand, choose, do.

To close, the OODA loop is Observe, Orient, Decide, Act, and it is a loop because each situation leads straight into the next. Observe spots what changed, Orient uses your knowledge to judge what the change means for safety, Decide picks the safest action, and Act carries it out smoothly with clear signals. Keep Observe and Orient separate: noticing a change is not the same as understanding what it means for you and others. To remember: observe, Orient, Decide, Act; orient is understanding; the loop never stops. A helpful hook for this lesson: notice, understand, choose, do.

why_how.text: Distractions can be inside the vehicle, outside it, physical or mental, and they make drivers drift and miss things.
No driver may hold an electronic device while driving, though hands-free use is permitted.

scenario.text: Zoe, an experienced adult driver, wants to check a map on her phone while driving.

reasoning.text: No driver of any age or experience may hold an electronic device while driving, though hands-free use is permitted.

result.text: Zoe may not hold the phone; she can use it hands-free or set the map before driving.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a distraction must involve a phone.

correction.text: Fatigue and discomfort are physical distractions, and daydreaming, worry and strong emotions are mental ones.

memory_support.text: Holding, not talking, is the line.

prompt.text: An experienced adult wants to hold a tablet to read directions while driving. Is that allowed?

answer.text: No, no driver may hold an electronic device while driving.

rationale.text: The law bans holding any electronic device while driving for every driver, while hands-free use stays permitted.

narration.text: This lesson covers distraction. The guide sorts distractions into four groups, describes how distracted drivers behave, and gives simple ways to avoid distraction. Then it turns to the law: how Washington defines distracted driving, what the device rule says, and how fines work. One key idea runs through the whole lesson: distraction is not only about phones, and the device law turns on holding a device, not on talking. To remember: four groups of distraction; effects and prevention; washington's device law. A helpful hook for this lesson: holding, not talking, is the line.

Distractions fall into four groups. Inside the vehicle, there are phones, food, the radio and passengers. Outside the vehicle, there are things like billboards and crashes. Physical distractions include fatigue or discomfort. Mental distractions include daydreaming, worry or strong emotion. So a driver can be distracted with the phone put away and the radio off, simply by being tired, uncomfortable, worried or lost in thought. To remember: inside: phones, food, radio, passengers; outside: billboards, crashes; physical and mental distractions.

lines.text: Myth: distraction always means a phone.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because phones get so much attention, many people think distraction always means a phone. The guide says otherwise. Fatigue and discomfort count as physical distractions, while daydreaming, worry and strong emotions are mental distractions. So a distraction need not involve a phone at all. When a question asks what kind of distraction something is, place it in one of the four groups rather than assuming it must involve a device. To remember: physical: fatigue, discomfort; mental: daydreaming, worry, emotion.

Distracted drivers tend to drift from their lane, drive too fast or too slow, miss signals, stop signs and vulnerable road users, and follow too closely. To avoid distraction, plan ahead, put the phone away and stay observant. The guide says this lets you react faster, decide better and feel less stress and fatigue. So preventing distraction is not only about avoiding tickets; it makes driving easier and less tiring. To remember: drifting, wrong speeds, missed signals; missing vulnerable road users; plan ahead; phone away.

lines.text: Any activity pulling attention from driving.
No driver may hold a device.

narration.text: Washington defines distracted driving as any activity that pulls attention away from the main job of driving. The device rule is specific. No driver of any age or experience may hold an electronic device such as a phone, tablet or gaming device while driving, though hands-free use is permitted. So the rule applies to every driver, from new to experienced, and the deciding line is whether the device is in your hand. A hands-free call is allowed; holding the phone, even to glance at a map, is not. To remember: any activity pulling attention from driving; no driver may hold a device; hands-free use is permitted.

An officer can ticket you for breaking the distracted driving law, and the fines can be heavy. Fines for violations after your first can be doubled. So the first ticket carries its own fine, and repeat violations can cost twice as much. Doubling applies to fines after your first violation, not to the first ticket itself. The penalties rise for drivers who keep breaking the rule, which gives repeat offenders a strong reason to change the habit. To remember: an officer can ticket you; fines can be heavy; later violations can be doubled.

Here is a quick check: an experienced adult driver wants to hold a tablet to read directions while driving. Is that allowed? Decide before the answer, and remember the line the law draws. Experience and age do not matter here. The answer is no. No driver of any age or experience may hold an electronic device while driving. Hands-free use is permitted, so the driver could use a mounted, hands-free setup, or set the route before driving. A helpful hook for this lesson: holding, not talking, is the line. In short: the law bans holding any electronic device while driving for every driver, while hands-free use stays permitted.

lines.text: Never hold a device; hands-free is allowed.

narration.text: To close, distractions can be inside the vehicle, outside it, physical such as fatigue, or mental such as worry, and distracted drivers drift, misjudge speed, miss signals and follow too closely. Plan ahead and put the phone away. Washington defines distracted driving as any activity that pulls attention from driving, and no driver may hold an electronic device while driving, though hands-free use is permitted. Tickets can bring heavy fines, and later violations can be doubled. To remember: inside, outside, physical, mental; never hold a device; hands-free is allowed; later fines can double.

why_how.text: Smart drivers are aware, in control, predictable, thoughtful and intentional in learning.
The guide names four kinds of attention: switching, divided, focused and sustained.

scenario.text: Ana is on a three-hour highway drive with little traffic.

reasoning.text: Sustained attention holds your focus over a long time.

result.text: Ana's long, quiet drive calls mainly on sustained attention.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking multitasking helps you drive more efficiently.

correction.text: The guide says to refuse to multitask and to remove distractions to help your attention.

prompt.text: Which kind of attention handles several things at once?

rationale.text: Divided attention handles several tasks at once, unlike focused attention on one task or sustained attention over time.

narration.text: This lesson looks at the habits of smart drivers and at attention itself. The guide describes five traits of smart drivers, names four kinds of attention you use behind the wheel, and lists practical ways to support your attention. Attention can sound like something you either have or do not, but the guide treats it as a set of skills that can be protected and strengthened. We will connect the four kinds of attention to real driving moments. To remember: traits of smart drivers; four kinds of attention; protecting your attention.

lines.text: Aware inside and outside the car.

narration.text: Smart drivers share several traits. They are aware inside and outside the car. They are in control of the gas, brake, steering and position. They are predictable, through signals and smooth moves. They are thoughtful in their decisions. And they are intentional in learning, always building their skills. These traits echo earlier lessons: awareness and predictability come up in the decision steps, and intentional learning ties to practicing safe habits. To remember: aware inside and outside the car; in control and predictable; thoughtful and intentional in learning.

The guide names four kinds of attention. Switching attention moves quickly from one focus to another. Divided attention is spread across several tasks at once. Focused attention puts your whole mind on one task. Sustained attention holds over a long time. Driving uses all four. You switch between mirrors and the road, divide attention between steering and scanning, focus on a tricky merge, and sustain attention on a long trip. To remember: switching between focuses; divided across tasks; focused; sustained over time.

lines.text: Trap: treating the four as one.
Sustained: held over a long time.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The four kinds of attention have similar names, so they are easy to mix up. Switching attention jumps quickly from one thing to another, divided attention handles several things at once, focused attention puts the whole mind on one task, and sustained attention holds it over a long time. When a question describes a driving moment, ask what the mind is doing: jumping, sharing, concentrating or holding steady. That points to the right type. To remember: divided: several things at once; sustained: held over a long time.

lines.text: Which attention type handles several tasks?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: which kind of attention handles several things at once? Decide before the answer, and use the trap's question: what is the mind doing? It is sharing itself among tasks. The answer is divided attention. Focused attention puts the whole mind on one task, switching attention jumps from one thing to another, and sustained attention holds steady over a long time. Each describes a different way your mind works while driving. A helpful hook for this lesson: switch, divide, focus, sustain. In short: divided attention handles several tasks at once, unlike focused attention on one task or sustained attention over time.

lines.text: Limit passengers and pets; no multitasking.

narration.text: The guide lists ways to help your attention. Remove in-car distractions. Be well rested before you drive. Mute and stow your electronics. Limit passengers and pets. And refuse to multitask. Each step takes something away from the competition for your attention, leaving more of it for driving. Refusing to multitask is especially important, because divided attention is already working hard just to handle the normal tasks of driving. To remember: remove in-car distractions; be well rested; stow electronics; limit passengers and pets; no multitasking.

To sum up, smart drivers are aware inside and outside the car, in control of gas, brake, steering and position, predictable through signals and smooth moves, thoughtful in decisions and intentional in learning. The four kinds of attention are switching, divided, focused and sustained. Help your attention by removing in-car distractions, being well rested, silencing and stowing electronics, limiting passengers and pets, and refusing to multitask. To remember: aware, in control, predictable; switching, divided, focused, sustained; remove distractions; no multitasking.

why_how.text: Searching uses your eyes, while scanning adds your head, neck and body to see as much as possible.
Drive at a speed that lets you search and scan well, because constant searching underpins safe driving.

scenario.text: Kim is driving past a row of parked cars on a residential street.

reasoning.text: Scanning ahead means watching for blockages that could hide people, such as feet, wheels or shadows near parked cars.

result.text: Kim watches under and between the parked cars for feet, wheels or shadows.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking searching and scanning mean the same thing.

correction.text: Searching uses your eyes alone, while scanning also moves your head, neck and body to widen what you see.

memory_support.text: Search with eyes; scan with your body.

prompt.text: You turn your head and shoulders to look around a corner. Are you searching or scanning?

rationale.text: Scanning adds turning your head, neck and body to searching with your eyes, so it widens what you can see.

narration.text: This lesson is about where and how to look while you drive. The guide separates two skills, searching and scanning, and stresses driving at a speed that allows both. Then it gives specific things to watch for ahead of you, to the side, and behind you, including when to look behind more often. These habits are the observation part of good decision-making, and they connect directly to the OODA loop you learned earlier in this section. To remember: searching and scanning; speed that allows scanning; ahead, sides and behind.

lines.text: Searching: actively checking with your eyes.
Scanning adds head, neck and body.

narration.text: Searching means actively checking around you with your eyes. Scanning adds turning your head, neck and body to see as much as possible. Both matter, and the guide ties them to speed: drive at a speed that still lets you search and scan well, because constant searching underpins safe driving. If you are going too fast to look around properly, your speed is too high for the situation, even if it is under the limit. To remember: searching: actively checking with your eyes; scanning adds head, neck and body; speed must allow both.

lines.text: Scanning: head, neck and body too.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Searching and scanning sound interchangeable, but the guide treats them as different skills. Searching uses your eyes alone to check around you, while scanning also moves your head, neck and body to widen what you can see. So a glance in the mirror with your eyes is searching, while turning your head and shoulders for a better view is scanning. When a question mentions body movement, the answer is scanning. To remember: searching: eyes alone; scanning: head, neck and body too. A helpful hook for this lesson: search with eyes; scan with your body.

lines.text: Feet, wheels or shadows near parked cars.
What is beyond the car in front.

narration.text: Scanning ahead means watching for things to steer around and for blockages that could hide people. Near parked cars, look for feet, wheels or shadows that could mean someone is about to step out. Also watch what is happening beyond the car in front, not just the car itself. Seeing farther ahead lets you avoid sudden braking or swerving, because you notice trouble early enough to respond smoothly. To remember: things to steer around; feet, wheels or shadows near parked cars; what is beyond the car in front. A helpful hook for this lesson: search with eyes; scan with your body.

lines.text: Mirror and shoulder check before turning.

narration.text: Scanning to the side means watching left and right at intersections and watching for crossing walkers and cyclists. It also means watching for movement behind foliage, where someone may be hidden. Before turning, do a mirror and over-shoulder check. So side scanning covers both the open view across an intersection and the hidden spaces, like bushes or the area beside your vehicle, that a quick look ahead would miss. To remember: left and right at intersections; crossing walkers and cyclists; mirror and shoulder check before turning.

lines.text: Before lane changes and bike-lane turns.
When slowing, backing or on steep hills.

narration.text: Look for vehicles and cyclists behind you before a lane change, before turning across a bike lane, and when slowing, backing, or heading down a long or steep hill. In heavy traffic, look behind more often. That way, a tailgater or fast-approaching vehicle gives you time to react by changing lanes, tapping the brakes, or adjusting your speed. Looking behind is not just for backing up; it protects you whenever your speed or path changes. To remember: before lane changes and bike-lane turns; when slowing, backing or on steep hills; more often in heavy traffic.

Here is a quick check: at a blind corner you turn your head and shoulders to look around it. Are you searching or scanning? Decide before the answer, and remember the difference. Searching uses your eyes alone. The answer is scanning. Scanning adds turning your head, neck and body to see as much as possible, which is exactly what you did. Both skills matter, and your speed should always leave you time to use them. A helpful hook for this lesson: search with eyes; scan with your body. In short: scanning adds turning your head, neck and body to searching with your eyes, so it widens what you can see.

lines.text: Search with eyes; scan with body.

narration.text: To close, searching means checking around you with your eyes, and scanning adds your head, neck and body. Drive at a speed that lets you do both. Scan ahead for things to steer around and for feet, wheels or shadows near parked cars, and look beyond the car in front. Scan to the side at intersections, for crossing walkers and cyclists and behind foliage, and check mirrors and shoulders before turning. Look behind before lane changes and when slowing, more often in heavy traffic. To remember: search with eyes; scan with body; speed that allows scanning; ahead, sides, behind.

why_how.text: Respectful driving means everyone buckled, being fit to drive, empathy, respecting space and avoiding conflict regardless of fault.
Road litter can cause crashes and wildfires, so littering fines are severe, and state law sets only the minimum fines.

scenario.text: Leo is hauling garden waste in an open truck bed to the dump.

reasoning.text: You and your passengers must secure loads and dispose of trash properly, because road litter can cause crashes.

result.text: Leo should cover and secure the load before driving.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking state law sets every littering rule everywhere in Washington.

correction.text: State law fixes only the minimum littering fines, and cities and counties may set different rules of their own.

memory_support.text: Secure the load, bin the trash.

prompt.text: Who should you ask about littering rules where you live?

answer.text: Local police, the sheriff, or a city or county clerk.

rationale.text: State law sets minimum fines and local ordinances may differ, so ask local police, the sheriff or a city or county clerk.

narration.text: This final lesson of the section looks beyond your own vehicle to the people and places around it. The guide describes what respectful driving means, how traffic advisories help you plan, and why littering is treated so seriously. It also covers idling, carbon monoxide and Washington's Clean Car Law. Finally, it asks you to evaluate your own driving after each trip. Together these ideas describe a driver who cares about safety, other people and the environment. To remember: respectful driving; advisories and litter; emissions and self-review.

lines.text: Avoid conflict; care for the environment.

narration.text: Respectful driving means everyone in the vehicle is buckled up and the driver is fit to drive. It means showing empathy and respecting others' space. It means avoiding conflict no matter who is at fault, rather than trying to prove a point. And it means caring for the road environment. So respect is not just politeness; it covers safety, attitude and the way you treat the world outside your car. To remember: everyone buckled; fit to drive; empathy and respect for space; avoid conflict; care for the environment. A helpful hook for this lesson: secure the load, bin the trash.

lines.text: Litter can cause crashes and wildfires.

narration.text: Road litter can cause crashes, and burning litter can start wildfires. For that reason, Washington's littering fines are severe. You and your passengers must secure loads and dispose of trash properly. State law sets minimum fines for littering and illegal dumping, and local ordinances may differ. To learn which rules apply where you are, ask local police, the sheriff, or a city or county clerk. To remember: litter can cause crashes and wildfires; severe littering fines; secure loads; dispose of trash. A helpful hook for this lesson: secure the load, bin the trash.

lines.text: Trap: state law sets every rule.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because the state sets littering fines, learners often assume state law is the whole story. State law fixes only the minimum littering fines, and cities and counties may set their own different rules on top of it. So the rules can vary from place to place. If a question asks who can tell you the local rules, the answer is local police, the sheriff, or a city or county clerk, not just the state. To remember: state: minimum fines only; cities and counties may differ. A helpful hook for this lesson: secure the load, bin the trash.

lines.text: Shut off when parked a while.
Newer cars must pass clean air standards.

narration.text: Leaving a parked car running, especially inside a garage, can release deadly carbon monoxide. So shut the engine off when parked for a while, drive smoothly, keep your tires inflated and carpool when you can. Washington's Clean Car Law says a vehicle built in or after the year the law names must pass strict clean air standards before anyone can register, license or sell it. A covered vehicle that fails cannot be registered, licensed or sold. To remember: idling can release carbon monoxide; shut off when parked a while; newer cars must pass clean air standards.

Here is a quick check: you want to know the littering rules that apply in your town. Whom should you ask? Decide before the answer, and remember that state law is not the whole picture. The state sets only the minimum fines. The answer is local police, the sheriff, or a city or county clerk. Local ordinances may differ from state law, so those local offices can tell you which rules apply where you live. A helpful hook for this lesson: secure the load, bin the trash. In short: state law sets minimum fines and local ordinances may differ, so ask local police, the sheriff or a city or county clerk.

The guide closes with self-evaluation. After or during a drive, ask yourself whether anything surprised you and whether you surprised anyone. Ask whether your driving was legal, proficient and smooth, and what you will change next time. The reason is simple: skills fade without review. A few honest questions after each drive keep your skills sharp and turn every trip into practice, which is the intentional learning that smart drivers rely on. To remember: did anything surprise you; did you surprise anyone; legal, proficient, smooth? What changes.

To sum up, respectful driving means everyone buckled, being fit, empathy, respecting space, avoiding conflict and caring for the environment. Traffic advisories warn of conditions and closures through signs, radio and apps. Litter can cause crashes and wildfires, so secure loads, dispose of trash, and check local rules beyond the state minimums. Avoid idling, especially in a garage, follow the Clean Car Law, and evaluate your driving after each trip, because skills fade without review. To remember: respect people and space; secure loads; check local rules; avoid idling; review your driving.
